title: Dynamical Mean-Field Theory for Real Materials using Variational Quantum Compressed Time Evolution on a Quantum Computer
authors: Stefan Wolf, Johannes Selisko, Timo Eckstein, Ludwig Nützel, Maximilian Amsler, Christopher Wever, Georgy Samsonidze, Thomas Eckl, Michael J. Hartmann
abstract: We design a hybrid quantum-classical computational workflow, combining density functional theory and dynamical mean-field theory, to investigate the electronic properties of CaCuO2, a parent structure of high-temperature cuprate superconductors. Our approach uses a quantum algorithm as an impurity solver that is based on variational quantum compressed time evolution to compute the time-dependent Greens function on an IBM Heron quantum device. Utilizing error mitigation techniques and a Lehmann representation fitting procedure, we extract the density of states from the signal in the accessible time regime. Despite the significant challenges rooted in the residual imprecision of currently accessible NISQ devices, we successfully resolve the characteristic features of the spectral function. However, we find that the required numerical accuracy for full DMFT self-consistency exceeds current hardware capabilities, indicating that practical real-material DMFT applications will necessitate post-NISQ hardware developments.
summary: This work proposes a quantum algorithm to solve the electronic properties of cuprate superconductors using a $	ext{DFT}+	ext{DMFT}$ framework. It utilizes variational quantum compressed time evolution to calculate the Green's function on a quantum computer. While it successfully resolves key spectral features, the authors conclude that full, self-consistent simulations require fault-tolerant, post-$	ext{NISQ}$ hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 1. DFT+DMFT workflow for CaCuO2. A DFT calculation (PBE) is downfolded onto a single-band Hub- bard model with interaction strength U = 3.11 eV. The DMFT equations are first converged with a CTHYB solver at β = 30 eV−1 and subsequently with an ED solver at T = 0 K, using an Anderson impurity model with two bath sites (⟲s.c. denotes self-consistent DMFT loops). The final ED-DMFT iteration is recomputed with the quantum impurity solver to obtain the density of states DOS(ω) and the quasiparticle weight Z.

Figure 2. Hadamard test for measuring the Green’s function G(t) using the approximation V (θn) = VL(θL n) . . . V1(θ1 n) with L layers of the Hamiltonian variational ansatz. The final layer is followed by an additional CP -gate and RZ-gates acting on the impurity sites (as illustrated here). The circuit for the ground state preparation UGS is obtained via VQE and a Hamiltonian variational ansatz.

Figure 3. Real (a) and imaginary (b) components of iG(t) obtained with the circuits using the VQA-Compression algorithm with L ∈{1, 2, 3} in a state-vector simulation. We compare our trained circuits to a first-order Trotter expansion with the same circuit depth as L = 3.
Figure 4. Real component of G0(t) evaluated on IBM Heron (ibm torino) for L ∈{1, 2, 3} compared to the exact analytic calculation showing the increase in damping dependent on L.

Figure 5. Real component of iG(t) obtained with the pretrained circuits using 65 two-qubit gates on the IBM Heron quantum computer without (a) and with (b) error mitigation. The number of shots is 8192 for each point in time.
